nature-econ-407.title: The price mechanism: how prices share out resources
nature-econ-407.text: When the 1970s oil crisis drove oil prices up, several countries started producing their own oil. That response is the price mechanism at work: the way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded. Prices match buyers and sellers in three ways: as an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources. The mechanism can be slow. Dearer fuel does not quickly cut demand, but over time it pushes firms to offer alternatives such as {{ref:nature-pol-305}} and electric cars. Once competition settles into balance, the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it, an ideal explored in {{ref:nature-econ-178}}. The mechanism takes many forms. In the form covered in {{ref:nature-econ-671}}, bidders compete and the highest bid wins. Cap-and-trade for planet-warming gases applies the idea to emissions, as the US did earlier with sulfur dioxide, cutting overall smog. Ludwig von Mises argued that planned economies reject the price mechanism and so cannot allocate resources rationally.

nature-econ-494.title: Income inequality: how unevenly income is shared
nature-econ-494.text: UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality. Income inequality is the extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population. It can be measured with tools such as the {{ref:nature-econ-873}} and the {{ref:nature-econ-527}}. Many economists argue that some inequality is necessary, but that excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice. Globalization complicates the picture. It tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

nature-econ-522.title: Fiscal policy: steering the economy with taxes and spending
nature-econ-522.text: Fiscal policy grew out of the Great Depression of the 1930s, when the earlier hands-off approach to managing the economy stopped working. It is a government's use of taxes and spending to influence the economy. It rests on Keynes's theory that changing taxes and government spending shifts {{ref:nature-econ-868}}, the total spending in an economy, and with it economic activity. Governments use it to steady the economy through the business cycle. Fiscal policy usually runs through a government department. Its partner, {{ref:nature-econ-560}}, handles the amount of money and interest rates, usually through a central bank. Spending can be paid for by taxes, by printing money, called seigniorage, or by borrowing at home or abroad. A deficit is often funded by issuing bonds, and if revenue cannot cover the interest, a nation may default. Developing countries collect about half as much tax as a share of GDP as developed countries, which limits their fiscal policy.

nature-econ-583.title: Purchasing power parity: comparing what money can buy
nature-econ-583.text: A computer costs 500 US dollars in New York and 2000 HK dollars in Hong Kong. If the same thing should cost the same everywhere, that implies 4 HK dollars per US dollar. This is purchasing power parity, or PPP. It compares currencies by what the same basket of goods costs in each country, giving an {{ref:nature-res-274}} based on purchasing power. It applies the law of one price to whole baskets. Economists use PPP to compare countries' GDP, output per worker, consumption and cost of living. The OECD's basket covers around 3,000 consumer goods and services, 30 government occupations, 200 types of equipment and about 15 construction projects. PPP suits comparisons of whole economies, where goods that are never traded matter, while market rates suit single traded goods. The calculations are disputed, because comparable baskets are hard to find and people in different countries buy different things. The global poverty line is converted between currencies with PPP rates, though high-end goods that poor people rarely buy skew them.

nature-econ-595.title: Carbon in the air as a stock and flow problem
nature-econ-595.text: The carbon dioxide in the air is a stock, measured in tons. Emissions raise it and sequestration, the capture and storage of carbon, lowers it, both measured in tons per day. Mathematically, a stock is the accumulation of inflows minus outflows over time. Seen this way, {{ref:nature-clim-149}} is a stock-and-flow problem: to shrink the stock of heat-trapping gases in the air, cut emissions and pull more carbon dioxide back out. {{ref:nature-eco-762}} is full of such problems, from the cycles of carbon, nitrogen and water to Earth's energy budget. Stocks and flows are also the building blocks of the models in {{ref:nature-es-077}}, where Jay Forrester called them levels and rates.

nature-econ-597.title: Greening the national accounts: a half-century effort
nature-econ-597.text: For decades, the world's standard rulebook for national accounts left out the natural world that holds the economy up. Critics argued that the System of National Accounts ignored the environment that contains and supports the economy. It did not value resource stocks, their running down, or ecosystem services. Leaving out pollution costs meant the accounts overstated the net benefits of economic activity. Change came slowly. SNA 1993 first introduced environmental side accounts linked to the main ones, described in {{ref:nature-econ-598}}. It also introduced a {{ref:nature-acct-119}} adjusted for resources used up, though not formally within the framework. The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, or SEEA, followed the {{ref:nature-hist-003}} in Rio in 1992, and its Central Framework became a UN standard in February 2012. SNA 2025 goes further. It formally recognizes natural capital and ecosystem services and treats the using up of resources as a cost of production. In early 2025 at least 94 countries had produced at least one SEEA account in the past five years, 67 of them regularly. The argument is not over. Environmentalists say the SNA still undervalues nature, while statisticians note that measurement methods remain unsettled.

nature-econ-599.title: Total factor productivity: the growth nobody can explain
nature-econ-599.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-256}} (1957) called it 'technical change', shorthand for any shift in the production function. Total factor productivity, or TFP, is the ratio of total output to total inputs: how much output a given bundle of inputs yields. Nobody measures it directly. Its growth is whatever part of output growth is left after counting growth in measured labour and capital, so it is calculated as a residual. For small changes, TFP growth is roughly output growth minus the growth of labour and capital inputs, usually weighted 0.7 for labour and 0.3 for capital. The leftover is large. Easterly and Levine estimated in 2001 that it accounts for 60 percent of growth in output per worker in an average country. Official statisticians prefer the name multifactor productivity, because inputs such as energy are left out, as are costs like the using up of minerals and pollution. Some economists consider TFP invalid, or at least in need of careful interpretation. Critics say it lacks meaningful units and may be a modelling artefact.

nature-econ-606.title: The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused
nature-econ-606.text: In 1833 the English economist Lloyd described herders sharing a common pasture. Each could add extra cattle, and together the extra cattle could lead to {{ref:nature-eco-761}}. The tragedy of the commons is the idea behind that scene. When people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up. The name comes from a 1968 essay in the journal Science by the ecologist Hardin, who took his title from Lloyd's pamphlet. Hardin's main worry was that there would be too many people, and he wrote that 'freedom in a commons brings ruin to all'. The idea now serves as a model for many resource problems, including water, forests, fish, and oil, gas and coal. Climate change has been described as a huge example, with the Earth treated as a commons depleted without regard to the harm done to others. Proposed government fixes include privatization, regulation such as permits for fishing or logging, and making users pay for the harm they cause. Whether the tragedy is inevitable is disputed. Ostrom and colleagues found it less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed, because local users often design their own rules. Farmers have run one Swiss Alpine commons since 1517. Critics add that historical English common land always had a legal owner, and only people with legal rights, called commoners, could use it.

nature-econ-629.title: The Coase theorem: bargaining away externalities
nature-econ-629.text: Two radio stations interfere with each other's signals. Ronald Coase, thinking about this case, saw that the station gaining more from broadcasting would simply pay the other not to interfere. From that came the Coase theorem: when one party's activity harms or helps another, the two can bargain to an efficient outcome whoever starts with the property rights, provided bargaining costs are low enough. If fencing the farm is cheaper than fencing the cattle, a fence should go around the farm whether the farmer or the rancher holds the rights. If true, the theorem would let private individuals solve externality problems by themselves. Coase himself did not think so. In his 1960 paper he argued that real transaction costs are rarely low enough for efficient bargaining. Imperfect information and poorly defined property rights can also block the bargain. In Danish talks between waterworks and farmers, farmers used their information advantage to seek over-compensation and drag out talks. Richard Thaler found that people care about fairness when bargaining over their own property, so they may reject efficient but unfair deals. The starting allocation of rights does not affect efficiency, but it does affect who ends up with the wealth, since the rights holder can extract payment from others. Critics argue the theorem rarely applies in practice, and Duncan Kennedy argues that the starting allocation of rights always matters.

nature-econ-648.title: The Environmental Goods Agreement: trade talks that collapsed
nature-econ-648.text: In 2015, 18 members of {{ref:nature-pol-007}} began talks to cut tariffs on goods used to protect the environment. In trade usage, 'environmental goods' means such products: {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} technology and pollution control systems, for example. The talks aimed to spread cleaner technologies for air pollution control, waste treatment, power from sources that replenish, monitoring and energy efficiency. They collapsed in 2016.

nature-econ-650.title: Georgism and the environment: pollution as a taking from the commons
nature-econ-650.text: To a Georgist, pollution is a taking from the commons, so its value should be captured for the public through taxes or quotas. Henry George partly inspired early conservation efforts in the Progressive Era, explored in {{ref:nature-hist-014}}. Georgists and ecological economists both favor market-based limits on pollution, but Georgists insist the income should not go to polluters. Their 'cap and share' would sell temporary pollution permits by bidding and give the proceeds to the public, instead of handing permits free to polluters. Some ecological economists also back a tax on land values, to free unused land for nature and curb {{ref:nature-pol-311}}.

nature-econ-671.title: Auctions: letting the highest bidder set the price
nature-econ-671.text: Each year the US EPA auctions about 250,000 allowances to the highest bidders, each letting its owner emit one ton of sulfur dioxide. An auction is a way of buying or selling by inviting bids and then dealing with the highest bidder, or, when buying, the lowest. The open ascending-price auction, where each bid must beat the one before, is probably the most common kind and has a long history. Auctions trade antiques, livestock, radio spectrum, used cars, real estate, online advertising and emission permits, among much else. Governments earn the most from spectrum and quota auctions: Russia's crab quota sold for €2 billion in 2019. Fishing quotas can be handed out free or auctioned when a catch-share scheme starts. The branch of economics that studies how auctions are designed and how bidders behave is {{ref:nature-pol-316}}. Paul Milgrom and Robert B. Wilson won the 2020 Nobel Prize for introducing new kinds of auction.

nature-econ-710.title: How can altruism evolve?
nature-econ-710.text: Darwin noticed a puzzle. If selection acts only on individuals, behavior that helps another at a cost to oneself makes no sense, yet many social animals behave altruistically. Game theory offers several routes out. Kin selection works through shared genes: Hamilton's rule says relatedness must exceed the ratio of cost to benefit. {{ref:nature-econ-077}} ('I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine') and its indirect form are further routes. Without some measure of reputation, only the direct form can arise in the prisoner's dilemma. Nowak and Wilson's group-selection explanation of insect colonies challenges the kin-selection account, and it is described as controversial.

nature-econ-757.title: Interest rates: the cost of money now instead of later
nature-econ-757.text: Firms borrow from banks expecting the borrowed capital to earn a return greater than the cost of the loan. That cost is set by the interest rate: the interest charged or paid each period, expressed as a share of the amount lent, deposited or borrowed. Rates are normally quoted per year. Total interest depends on the rate together with the principal, the sum originally lent, and on how often interest compounds and for how long. At heart, a rate reflects a borrower's willingness to pay for money now rather than money in the future. When rates change, the opportunity cost of funding new projects rises or falls for firms. Risk matters too. Riskier choices such as shares and high-risk 'junk' {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} normally have to promise higher returns than safer government bonds. Banks themselves live on the spread, the lending rate minus the deposit rate, which covers their operating costs.

nature-econ-777.title: Ambiguity aversion: preferring the odds you know
nature-econ-777.text: One urn holds 50 red and 50 black balls. Another holds 100 balls in an unknown mix. Asked to bet, people prefer the first urn. This result, known as {{ref:nature-econ-880}}, first revealed ambiguity aversion: a preference for risks whose odds are known over risks whose odds are unknown. It differs from risk aversion, which compares a gamble with its expected value when the odds are known. Risk aversion is mainly put down to diminishing marginal utility, but ambiguity aversion has no widely accepted main cause. It has been used to explain incomplete contracts, swings in share prices and selective abstention in elections. Greater ambiguity aversion also raises demand for insurance, as people dislike unknown events affecting their lives and property. Experiments suggest attitudes to ambiguity depend on context, so a measure from one setting may not predict behavior in another.

nature-econ-851.title: Progressive tax: rates that rise with income
nature-econ-851.text: Under a progressive tax, the rate climbs as the taxable amount grows, so a taxpayer's average rate stays below the marginal rate. The marginal rate is the one on each extra unit of income. The effective marginal rate is higher still once lost welfare benefits and tax credits are counted. A progressive tax shifts the burden toward people with more ability to pay. Its opposite is a {{ref:nature-pol-124}}, such as a sales tax, where the poor pay a larger share of income. It directly reduces {{ref:nature-econ-850}}, especially when it funds transfers and safety nets, though more evasion at higher rates may mute the effect. Brackets that are not indexed to inflation cause bracket creep, an effective tax increase. The effect on growth is disputed. A 2008 OECD report found a weak negative relationship, while the IMF says some advanced economies could raise progressivity without hampering growth. Hayek and Nozick opposed it on principle.

nature-econ-867.title: The Malthusian growth model: growth in proportion to size
nature-econ-867.text: In 1798 Thomas Malthus wrote his Essay on the Principle of Population, and one of the simplest models in biology bears his name. In the Malthusian growth model, a population's growth is proportional to its current size. It is often called the exponential or Malthusian law, and builds on {{ref:nature-econ-442}}. Its parameters are the initial population P0 and the growth rate r, which Fisher called the Malthusian parameter and Lotka the {{ref:nature-eco-586}}. {{ref:nature-eco-375}} treats it as the first principle of {{ref:nature-eco-585}}, by analogy with Newton's first law of motion. Malthus held that life tends to grow exponentially when resources are abundant, but actual growth is limited by available resources. Verhulst, after reading the essay, developed a population model bounded by resource limits in 1838 and named it the logistic function.

nature-econ-868.title: Aggregate demand: the economy's total shopping list
nature-econ-868.text: Aggregate demand is the total demand for final goods and services in an economy at a given time, in other words demand for a country's GDP. It is made up of consumer spending, investment, government expenditure and net exports. Consumption is modelled as C = C0 + c(Y−T), with autonomous consumption C0, the {{ref:nature-econ-872}} c and disposable income Y−T. Only planned investment counts. Unplanned inventory build-up signals a demand shortfall and, in the Keynesian model, falling output and income. The curve plots real output against the price level. Its downward slope comes from Pigou's wealth effect, the Keynes interest-rate effect and the Mundell–Fleming exchange-rate effect, not from individual rational behavior. Rightward shifts come from more money supply, government spending, autonomous investment or consumption, or lower taxes. In the AD–AS model, an increase raises mainly output when resources are idle, but increasingly prices as output nears potential. Keynes argued during the Great Depression that government spending should fill the loss of private demand. Austrian critics such as Hazlitt reject the concept as meaningless, and Hayek argued recessions have microeconomic causes.

nature-econ-870.title: The business cycle: booms, busts and their rhythms
nature-econ-870.text: Economies do not grow smoothly. The business cycle is intervals of general expansion followed by recession. The simplest definition calls a recession two consecutive quarters of negative growth in {{ref:nature-econ-483}}; better ones use more indicators, such as consumer confidence, retail trade, unemployment and production indexes. Burns and Mitchell's 1946 standard definition stresses that the fluctuations are widely diffused across the economy. Sismondi's 1819 work was the first systematic account of crises. Classical economics had denied cycles, blamed external factors such as war, or studied only the long term. Juglar first identified cycles of 7 to 11 years in 1860, and later work found Kondratiev waves in world GDP and Kuznets cycles of about 17 years. Commodity price shocks are considered a significant driver of the US cycle, and a majority of post-war recessions are linked to oil price rises. Since the 1940s most developed-nation governments have treated softening the cycle as their responsibility under {{ref:nature-econ-554}}.

nature-econ-872.title: Marginal propensity to consume: what an extra dollar does
nature-econ-872.text: Give someone one more dollar of disposable income and see how much they spend: that share is the marginal propensity to consume, the change in consumption divided by the change in income. With a value of 0.65, an extra dollar brings 65 cents spent and 35 saved. It is usually between 0 and 1, but can exceed 1 if the person borrows or draws down savings, and can fall below zero if higher income prompts saving for a purchase. One minus it is the {{ref:nature-econ-589}} in a two-sector closed economy, a key determinant of the multiplier. Keynes held it is below one, and higher for poorer people than for rich ones. The Keynesian multiplier should be larger for permanent than for temporary income changes, though telling them apart is often hard.

nature-econ-875.title: Kin selection: helping relatives at a cost
nature-econ-875.text: {{ref:nature-eco-745}} can favor a trait that costs the organism but helps its relatives. This is kin selection, and it can lead to altruistic behaviour. It is tied to inclusive fitness, which counts offspring produced and those an individual helps produce, weighted by relatedness. Hamilton's 1964 rule says a behaviour spreads when relatedness times the benefit to the recipient exceeds the cost to the actor. Altruism can be favoured by kin recognition, or in 'viscous' populations with limited dispersal, where neighbours are usually relatives. Humans favour kin, for example in wills in proportion to relatedness, though many evolutionary psychologists warn that relatedness is not the same as shared genes. Critics such as Alonso and Wilson, and Nowak and Tarnita, dispute inclusive fitness theory.

nature-econ-878.title: Dynamic inconsistency: when today's plan fails tomorrow
nature-econ-878.text: People tend to choose 500 dollars today over 505 tomorrow, yet 505 dollars in 366 days over 500 in 365 days. The two choices cannot both be right. This is dynamic inconsistency: preferences change over time, so an earlier plan conflicts with what the person wants later. It can be pictured as many 'selves' at different times whose preferences are not aligned. {{ref:nature-econ-034}} theorists say dynamic inconsistency, behavioral economists say time inconsistency. {{ref:nature-econ-794}}, with a constant {{ref:nature-econ-747}}, yields time-consistent preferences. Empirical research suggests time inconsistency is standard in human preferences, and a stronger weight on 'now' is called the immediacy effect. See {{ref:nature-econ-748}}. Procrastination, addiction, weight loss and saving for retirement all rely on this idea. In that field, a player's best plan for a future period may not be optimal when it arrives, so threats lack credibility. A firm cannot commit its future self to a price war against an entrant. Commitment mechanisms limit future agency, as Odysseus did by tying himself to the mast. Independent central banks serve the same role against inflation promises (Kydland and Prescott, 1977).

nature-econ-880.title: The Ellsberg paradox: why we shun unknown odds
nature-econ-880.text: Keynes published a version in 1921, and Daniel Ellsberg popularised it in his 1961 paper 'Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms'. In the two-urn test, urn A holds 50 red and 50 black balls and urn B an unknown mix. People are indifferent between red and black within each urn, yet strictly prefer bets on urn A. In the one-urn test, 30 of 90 balls are red and 60 are black or yellow in unknown proportion. People prefer Gamble A to B and Gamble D to C, which no single probability belief can explain. The result holds whatever the utility function or risk aversion, because the exact odds are known for Gambles A and D but not for B and C. Most read it as {{ref:nature-econ-777}}. Choquet and {{ref:nature-econ-778}} are proposed responses; another explanation is deceit aversion, where people assume an unstated probability hides a trick.

nature-econ-881.title: Demurrage currency: money that melts
nature-econ-881.text: Local stamp scrip was used in at least 450 US cities in the Great Depression, and it had a feature ordinary money lacks: it lost value on purpose. A demurrage currency loses purchasing power gradually at a constant rate. Followers of Silvio Gesell hold that money's roles as store of value and medium of exchange conflict, so money that decays is best for exchange and discourages hoarding. Unlike {{ref:nature-econ-801}}, it reduces only the value of currency held, not newly issued money or claims such as stocks and bonds, and it does not raise consumer prices. Felix Fuders argues the {{ref:nature-eecon-178}} stems from interest burdens, and Bernard Lietaer says interest pushes resource use past what is ecologically optimal, such as cutting trees early. The Chiemgauer, started in Bavaria in 2003, carried a 6 percent annual rate in 2021. Keynes called stamped money sound but thought competing liquid money would evade the fees. A main barrier is trust.

nature-eecon-085.title: Ecologically unequal exchange: trade that drains the South
nature-eecon-085.text: Half of all materials consumed by high-income countries are extracted from poorer countries, Dorninger and colleagues found, while the rich countries still run trade surpluses. The ecological form of {{ref:nature-eecon-133}} is the idea that world trade hides an unfair flow of materials, energy and environmental damage, not just labor, from poorer to richer countries. It builds on world-systems theory, which splits the world economy into a rich core and a poorer periphery. Southern countries serve as sources of raw materials, sinks for waste and places written off as a {{ref:nature-gov-224}}. A study of EU consumption from 1995 to 2019 found much of its environmental impact outsourced abroad, while more than 80% of the economic benefits stayed home. The logical result is an {{ref:nature-gov-199}} owed by North to South. Jason Hickel proposes {{ref:nature-eecon-143}} in the North to end it. Most cited studies support the theory, but Peter Somerville calls it confused and internally inconsistent.

nature-eecon-185.title: Overconsumption: using up faster than nature refills
nature-eecon-185.text: By 1983 China's consumption had already surpassed the biocapacity of its natural resources. Growing economies can drive overconsumption: using goods, services or natural resources faster than they can be replenished or reused. Applied to natural resources harmed by use, it means the same as {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. The drivers are partly built into how business works. Consumerism, {{ref:nature-eecon-188}}, economic materialism and other unsustainable business models push consumption up. It stands in contrast to {{ref:nature-eecon-196}}. Over the long term, overconsumption in a region shrinks natural resources and degrades the environment. Consuming beyond the environment's long-term {{ref:nature-eco-593}} causes {{ref:nature-eecon-173}}, resource depletion and poorer ecosystem health. In 2010 the International Resource Panel found that household consumption for mobility, shelter, food and energy-using products causes most of the life-cycle impacts of consumption. Movements push back: anti-consumerism, {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}, frugality, downshifting, {{ref:nature-eecon-254}} and minimalism. Many of them aim at a {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}. Even so, the term itself is controversial and lacks a single agreed definition.

nature-eecon-238.title: Energy: the quantity that is conserved and dissipated
nature-eecon-238.text: Energy is conserved. The total energy of an isolated system stays constant, though it can change form. {{ref:nature-eecon-114}} says the same of a closed system: its energy is constant unless transferred in or out as work or heat. Energy is the quantitative property transferred to a body or system, seen in the capacity to do work and in heat and light. Its SI unit is the joule, the work done by one newton over one metre. Power, energy per unit time, is measured in watts, one joule per second. Total energy divides into potential and kinetic energy, and forms such as mechanical or nuclear energy are combinations of the two. In irreversible processes energy is dissipated into available states and cannot be recovered into more concentrated forms without degrading more energy. Living things need an external source: sunlight for green plants, chemical energy for animals. Cellular respiration stores energy in carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. Sunlight is the main input to Earth's energy budget, which accounts for its temperature and climate stability.

nature-eecon-247.title: Urban metabolism: the city as a flow of materials
nature-eecon-247.text: Abel Wolman coined the term in 1965 by modelling the inflows and outflows of a hypothetical American city of 1 million people, mainly water and the waste it produces. Urban metabolism is now a model for describing the flows of materials and energy through cities, as in a city-level {{ref:nature-eecon-019}}. Herbert Girardet contrasted circular metabolism, where nearly everything is reused, with the linear metabolism of cities, with clear resource inputs and waste outputs. Howard T. Odum's energy method coined {{ref:nature-eecon-099}}, which measures the solar energy used directly or indirectly to make a product, in solar equivalent joules. Tracking materials became the mainstream school because its units are more practical for the public, officials and researchers. Planners use it for four things: sustainability reporting, urban greenhouse gas accounting, mathematical modelling for policy analysis and urban design.

nature-eecon-256.title: Robert Solow: growth from technical progress
nature-eecon-256.text: Robert Solow is the American economist behind the Solow-Swan growth model, and he won the 1987 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. His model separates the determinants of growth into increases in inputs (labour and capital) and technical progress. It is called exogenous because the saving rate is taken as given. Using it, Solow (1957) calculated that about four-fifths of the growth in US output per worker came from technical progress. Ecological economics places his strongly neoclassical position, with Martin Weitzman's, at one end of a continuum of views on weak versus {{ref:nature-eecon-218}}. Georgescu-Roegen and Daly stand at the other. Solow also criticised the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth as having 'simplistic' scenarios.

nature-es-092.title: Erosion control: keeping soil in place with plants
nature-es-092.text: New Deal programs in the United States planted 18,000 miles of tree and shrub belts to break the wind, from North Dakota to Texas, to fight soil erosion. Erosion control is the set of practices that prevent or repair soil erosion, chiefly by keeping land covered with plants. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent erosion by both wind and water. Terracing, cutting slopes into level steps, is a highly effective method practiced for thousands of years around the world. Such belts along fields also improve growing conditions around the crops, shelter birds and store carbon. {{ref:nature-nbs-355}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-276}} and leaving crop residues on the field under {{ref:nature-nbs-291}} all reduce erosion. {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, which mixes crops with trees, works especially well in rainy tropical climates. On coasts, the roots of the trees covered in {{ref:nature-eco-410}} slow water, trap sediment and bind soils. Good erosion control manages surface runoff and helps prevent water pollution, the loss of soil and habitat, and damage to property.

nature-found-004.title: Ecosystem services: the work nature does for people
nature-found-004.text: New York City had two ways to keep its water clean. It could build a filtration plant, estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run. Or it could restore its Catskill watershed, the land whose streams feed the city's supply, for an estimated $1–1.5 billion. The city chose the land, and the land did the plant's job for a fraction of the cost. That job is an ecosystem service: one of the many benefits people get from ecosystems. Others include pollination of crops, clean air, the breakdown of wastes and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control. These services are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and a steady climate. The term "environmental services" appeared in a 1970 report, and "ecosystem services" later became the standard term in science. In the early 2000s a United Nations initiative, covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. Economists value these services in dollars using methods such as avoided cost, the cost of replacing a service, travel cost and surveys of what people would pay. A 1997 study put the value of the world's ecosystem services and the natural stocks behind them at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion. Some schemes now reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it keeps providing a service, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-mkt-136}}.

nature-found-005.title: Four kinds of help: sorting ecosystem services
nature-found-005.text: Not every benefit from nature works the same way. Some touch nearby people directly, like fresh water or food. Others act through general conditions, like a steady climate or soil held in place against erosion. To keep track, scientists sort ecosystem services into groups. The best-known scheme, from a United Nations assessment, uses four: regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting. The provisioning group holds the products obtained from ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, wood, fibre and fuel. The regulating group comes from nature keeping its processes in check, through climate control, carbon storage, flood control and disease control. The supporting group, such as nutrient cycling and the making of soil, allows the other three to exist; it is the base on which the rest stand. Each group gets its own entry, beginning with {{ref:nature-found-009}}. An ecosystem need not offer all four kinds at once, but people usually benefit from a mix of them. Other schemes redraw the lines. To avoid counting the same benefit twice, a later study, covered in {{ref:nature-hist-001}}, replaced the base layer with habitat services. The Common International Classification for Ecosystem Services keeps the cultural and provisioning groups. It merges regulating and habitat services into one group, {{ref:nature-val-107}} and maintenance services.

nature-found-006.title: Provisioning services: food, timber and fuel from the wild
nature-found-006.text: In 2018, global production and {{ref:nature-res-268}} of all major wood-based products reached their highest recorded values. Wood is one of many provisioning services: the products people obtain from ecosystems. They include food such as crops, seafood, game and spices. They also include raw materials such as lumber, skins, fuelwood, fodder for animals and {{ref:nature-eco-662}}.

nature-found-015.title: The ecosystem, from a rock's surface to the whole planet
nature-found-015.text: An ecosystem can be as small as the surface of a single rock or as large as the surface of the planet. That is a span of ten orders of magnitude, and one idea covers all of it. An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings, linked by flows of {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} and nutrients. Plants are living, or biotic, parts; soil is a non-living, or abiotic, part. The flow begins when plants capture sunlight, a process traced in {{ref:nature-eco-190}}. Animals carry matter and the captured power onward by eating plants and one another. Other organisms break down dead matter and return its nutrients to the system. Some forces act from outside: climate shapes an ecosystem without being changed by it. Others act from within, such as the breakdown of dead matter and the mix of species present, which both shape the system and respond to it. No ecosystem stands still. Each is always recovering from past upsets, and its ability to absorb a shock and keep working is the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-603}}. The word itself is young. British ecologist Arthur Tansley first used it in 1935; Arthur Roy Clapham coined it at his request. Ecosystems matter to the economy because they supply goods, such as water, food, fuel and medicinal plants. They also supply services, such as clean air and water, oxygen and crop pollination. Many are now degraded by soil loss, pollution, invading species and habitats broken into fragments. One that has lost its defining features is called collapsed.

nature-found-026.title: Short-termism: the pull of the quick payoff
nature-found-026.text: Some actions take longer than one government's term to show results, and short-termism can undermine them. Short-termism is favouring quick profits and short-term results over long-term results and far-sighted action. It is linked to a thinking habit that prefers short-term payoffs to long-term rewards, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-065}}. Short-termism and {{ref:nature-eecon-249}} are named among the barriers to sustainability.

nature-found-027.title: Eco-capitalism: putting markets to work for nature
nature-found-027.text: Eco-capitalism, or green {{ref:nature-econ-848}}, starts from a claim: nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends. If that is true, markets should be used to solve environmental problems. Its supporters want governments to use market-based tools, such as a tax on carbon. A central aim is to correct a basic flaw in markets, in which polluters do not pay for the pollution they cause. Critics, including eco-socialists, doubt the approach. They argue that growth, and turning nature into a {{ref:nature-res-264}}, cannot easily be reconciled with {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

nature-found-029.title: Managing the planet's land, water and air for the long run
nature-found-029.text: Feeding humanity takes about 38% of Earth's land surface and about 20% of its net primary productivity, the new plant growth its ecosystems produce. Since the Neolithic Revolution, human consumption has cut the world's forest cover by about 47%. Sustainability and environmental management means running the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale by sustainability principles. How land is split between cities, farms, forest and {{ref:nature-nbs-350}} strongly affects the global cycles of water, carbon and nitrogen. Biodiversity loss stems largely from habitat loss, as natural capital is converted into man-made capital.

nature-found-041.title: Environmentally harmful subsidies: paying to use nature up
nature-found-041.text: Some government payments reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them. The damage these environmentally harmful subsidies do to nature has been conservatively estimated at $4-$6 trillion U.S. dollars per year. The largest support the fossil fuel, farming and water sectors.

nature-found-047.title: Failure of competition: when one firm holds the cards
nature-found-047.text: In a failure of market rivalry ({{ref:nature-econ-363}}), a firm or small group gains enough power over a market to block trades that would benefit both sides. This kind of market failure takes several forms: a market with a single seller, one with a single buyer, and markets where sellers compete with slightly different products. Such power can last where {{ref:nature-econ-863}} keep other firms out. An extreme case is a natural sole-seller market, a form of what {{ref:nature-econ-349}} describes, sometimes caused by extreme economies of scale, the cost advantages that come with sheer size.

nature-found-060.title: Ground-level ozone: the smog of hot afternoons
nature-found-060.text: Ozone near the ground peaks on hot summer afternoons. It forms mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, carbon-based vapours, react in sunlight. Ground-level ozone is the main gas in {{ref:nature-found-105}}, the haze that sunlight makes from these pollutants. It harms human health, materials, forests and crops, and it slows plants' capture of energy from sunlight. One study estimated that a 1% rise in ozone concentrations would cause a global economic loss of $10 billion each year.

nature-found-061.title: From black smoke as prosperity to cleaner air
nature-found-061.text: During the Industrial Revolution, coal burning raised outdoor pollution sharply. Yet city leaders saw black smoke as a sign of prosperity. Early laws against pollution were weak, because they were seen to clash with industrial interests. Disaster forced the turn. A thick fog of coal smoke over London in 1952 killed some 12,000 people and led to a new clean air law in 1956. Later problems crossed borders. Acid rain needed international cooperation, and ozone-damaging chemicals were later phased out by negotiation.

nature-found-064.title: Government failure: when the fix falls short
nature-found-064.text: Government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short. Government failure is the economic waste that results, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative. It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none. It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses; simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure. Any form of intervention can fail: provision, taxes or subsidies, and regulation. Common mechanisms include regulators coming to serve the industries they oversee, {{ref:nature-eco-740}}, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones. A small, well-organized interest group, for instance, can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole. The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s. Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures. Some economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.
